newsitem.title: PERU: Peru prepares for talks with hostage takers.
newsitem.headline: Peru prepares for talks with hostage takers.

text.p: Peru's government prepared on Saturday to sit down with Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima to discuss a peaceful end to the 25-day crisis.

After nearly two weeks of stalled negotiations, Education Minister Domingo Palermo spoke with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini on Friday to arrange a meeting at the besieged residence over the weekend.
The pair has not met since a first meeting on Dec. 28 when 20 hostages were freed.

Palermo, President Alberto Fujimori's appointed negotiator, gave no clues as to how he hoped to overcome the main sticking point in the crisis: the rebels' insistence that the government free about 400 jailed comrades. Fujimori has rejected this demand.
Palermo also insisted the government would accept nothing short of the release of all the remaining captives.

"My goal is to free the 74 hostages in their entirety, in good health and as quickly as possible," Palermo told foreign correspondents who witnessed his four-minute, walkie-talkie conversation with the guerrilla leader.
News of the renewed talks was greeted as a breakthrough in Tokyo, where concern was still high for about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen held by the gunmen.
"The mood has changed. Until now it has been a stalemate, but ... it seems there is some movement," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.
Palermo and Cerpa were polite and good-humoured in their contact, witnessed by correspondents from Reuters, the Italian news agency ANSA, Agence France-Presse and Mexican TV channel ECO.

In what they called "goodwill gestures" the heavily-armed group of about 15 MRTA rebels have freed more than 430 of the captives they seized after storming an exclusive cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.

But the rebels still held those they considered the best bargaining chips for negotiations with the government, including top government and security force officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro.
Fujimori has said the rebels could be offered safe passage to another country if they laid down their arms and released the captives under the supervision of a "guarantor committee".
The Peruvian leader hailed the talk with Cerpa as a "good sign" that raised "hopeful prospects" of a bloodless end to the crisis.
Palermo said he kept Fujimori constantly up to date, speaking with him up to 30 times a day.
Although he has not met Cerpa since Dec. 28, Palermo said they had stayed in contact via short, handwritten messages delivered by Red Cross officials.

Red Cross spokesman Steven Anderson said on Saturday that as well as attending to the hostages' basic needs the organisation "served as a channel at the disposition of the government and the MRTA to facilitate a solution to the crisis."

Anderson told local CPN radio the Red Cross had exchanged more than 2,000 written messages between the hostages and their families. The notes were "an important psychological support" to help them through the long ordeal, he said.
Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, invited by Cerpa to celebrate Mass inside the residence, said on Saturday: "I am optimistic that everything will turn out well."
About 20 MRTA rebels entered a small jungle village Friday to demand food and spread propaganda, local radio reported.
In the first such action for several months, a rebel unit of 13 men and seven women woke up residents of Palcazu in the central Pasco region, around dawn, CPN radio said.
They collected food, gave speeches about the hostage stand-off and painted slogans on walls.
The MRTA's armed members, estimated to number 250 at most after several years of decline, are mainly based in Peru's central jungle area.
